title: The Azahar Project: Non-Thermal Physics Drives Star Formation Burstiness and the Evolution of the UV Luminosity Density at Cosmic Dawn
hook: JWST keeps finding early galaxies too bright and fast-growing for standard simulations — a new suite finally reproduces them, and the fix is radiation pressure and cosmic rays, not supernovae.
key_points: JWST has found early-universe galaxies brighter and faster-growing than standard simulations predict.
The Azahar suite runs 10 high-resolution cosmological simulations that add ever more realistic physics.
Its 'Non-Thermal' model adds radiative transfer (starlight pressure) and cosmic rays to gas and gravity.
That model matches observed galaxy brightness from redshift ~14 down to cosmic noon (z~3).
It works via burstier star formation and outflows that weaken as cosmic-ray pressure builds up.
Boosted-supernova-only models fail: they overproduce stars or blow overly puffy galaxies.
content_html: Since JWST turned its eye on the earliest galaxies, it's kept finding ones that are unexpectedly bright and growing fast — too fast for standard galaxy-formation simulations to explain. A new suite of simulations finally reproduces them, and the fix isn't more supernovae: it's radiation pressure from starlight and cosmic rays reshaping how galaxies form stars.
extra_html: Sergio Martin-Alvarez, Risa Wechsler, and Debora Sijacki's team built Azahar, ten high-resolution cosmological simulations that progressively add radiative transfer, cosmic rays, and magnetic fields on top of standard gas-and-gravity physics. Their "Non-Thermal" version — radiative transfer plus cosmic rays together — matches observed galaxy brightness from redshift 14 down to cosmic noon (z~3), plus how total stellar mass and gas chemistry evolve over that stretch. The trick: burstier star formation, and outflows that weaken over time as cosmic-ray pressure builds inside galaxies. Models that just boost supernova feedback overproduce stars or blow galaxies into unrealistically puffy shapes, because they're missing these several distinct, differently-timed feedback channels.

related.title: Why Does Webb Keep Finding Things That Shouldn't Exist?
related.hook: JWST keeps spotting early black holes and galaxies that are too big, too bright, or too early to fit standard models — and cosmologists are racing to figure out which of many new theories is right.

related.title: 31 Quasars That Are Too Old to Make Sense
related.hook: Astronomers found 31 quasars shining from when the universe was just 5% of its current age — powered by black holes that shouldn't have had time to grow so big yet.

flashcards.prompt: What has JWST found about early-universe galaxies that puzzled existing simulations?
flashcards.back_html: Galaxies far brighter and faster-growing than standard galaxy-formation simulations predicted for the very early universe.

flashcards.prompt: What does the Azahar Project's 'Non-Thermal' model add on top of standard gas-and-gravity physics?

choices.text: Radiative transfer (starlight pressure) and cosmic rays, together
Nothing — it uses the same physics as older simulations

flashcards.explanation_html: The Non-Thermal model adds radiative transfer and cosmic rays together, which is what lets it match the galaxies JWST is actually seeing.

flashcards.prompt: Why do simple 'boosted supernova' models fail to match early JWST galaxies?
flashcards.back_html: They lack the distinct non-thermal feedback channels, so they either overproduce stellar mass or blow galaxies into overly puffy, unrealistic outflows.
